title: Women in the teaching
hookLine: the Gurus honored women as equals, as teachers and as leaders
last: THE SAME LIGHT IN EVERY SOUL.

lines: THE PLAIN FACTS OF A LIFE.
cards: Why call her bad? The question comes from Guru Nanak, in the middle of a long hymn.

Around him, a woman could be treated as a lesser thing: unclean at certain times, blamed for misfortune, expected in some places to follow her husband into the fire when he died. Guru Nanak doesn't start with a rule.
He starts with the plain facts of a life. Who carries the child? Who is a man engaged to, married to, befriended by?
Who keeps the family going when someone dies? And then the question lands: why call her bad, from whom kings are born?

teach.h: ASA DI VAR: WHY CALL HER BAD?
teach.b: First, the hymn. It sits in Asa di Var, the morning hymn sung in gurdwaras. In paraphrase: from woman we are born, in woman we are conceived, to woman we are engaged and married; through woman the generations go on.
So why call her bad, from whom kings are born? It's an argument from the kitchen table, not from a throne. Second, a woman at the hearth.
The Granth keeps a hymn by the bards Balwand and Satta praising Mata Khivi, the wife of Guru Angad. In paraphrase: Khivi was good, her shade cool and leafy, and she gave out rich sweet rice to all.

Tradition remembers her running the Guru's langar, so the kitchen where yesterday's equality became dinner had a woman at its center. Third, a custom refused. You met this early on the path, with the manjis.

teach.h: GURU AMAR DAS REFUSES THE PYRE.
teach.b: Guru Amar Das speaks against the burning of widows; in paraphrase from a salok: those who burn with their husband's body are not truly sati; the true ones live on in love and goodness.
Tradition also says he appointed women among the teachers he sent out. Fourth, leaders.
Sikh memory holds Mata Gujri, mother of Guru Gobind Singh, steady through the hardest days, and Mai Bhago, who tradition says rallied men who had turned back and rode out with them.
Teachers, cooks, mothers, leaders. And it's honest to add: the teaching is clear, and living up to it in every gurdwara and family is still a work in progress.

how: In gurdwaras women and men can lead kirtan, read from the Guru Granth Sahib and serve in the langar; Sikhs remember women such as Mata Khivi, Mata Gujri and Mai Bhago.

games.q: what does “women in the teaching” mean?
o: rules that keep women out of the gurdwara kitchen
a set of hymns that only women may sing aloud
the Gurus honored women as equals, teachers and leaders

the Granth never names a woman
Balwand and Satta's hymn praises Mata Khivi and her sweet rice.

he said the true ones live on in love and goodness.

games.q: you're Guru Amar Das, and the custom says a widow should follow her husband into the fire. what do you say?
o: praise her courage, as the custom does.
stay silent; it's a family matter.
say the true sati lives on in love and goodness.
games.why: his salok says those who burn with the body are not truly sati; living on in love is the true way.

practice: Bring to mind a woman who taught you something real: a grandmother, a teacher, a neighbor, a boss, a friend.
Hear one thing she said, in her own voice, and breathe in with it; breathe out and let it land again, as if for the first time.
If nobody comes to mind, recall a woman's words you've read or heard, a talk or a book, and let those land instead.

wordCard.voice: Women in the teaching. The Gurus honored women as equals: Guru Nanak's why call her bad, Mata Khivi at the langar, and Guru Amar Das refusing the widow's pyre. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: equals. Why call her bad, from whom kings are born? That's today, done.
